\title{Customary Prices and the Militia:
The Grain Riots of 1817 in the Upper Rhine Valley}
\author{E.~Vogel}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
This article re-examines the grain price riots that swept the
market towns of the upper Rhine valley in the spring of 1817,
the so-called year without a summer. Drawing on guild records,
municipal account books, and the correspondence of district
magistrates, it argues that the riots were not spontaneous
outbursts of hunger but carefully negotiated performances in
which crowds enforced customary price ceilings while avoiding
direct confrontation with the militia. The article reconstructs
three riot days in the town of Freiburg, traces the kinship
networks of the identified ringleaders, and compares official
bread-price ordinances with prices recorded in bakers' ledgers.
It concludes that customary economy and state paternalism
coexisted longer than the standard narrative allows.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
The spring of 1817 brought the worst subsistence crisis of the
nineteenth century to the lands between the Vosges and the
Black Forest.
Harvest failures following the Tambora eruption had doubled the
price of rye within a single winter, and by April the market
squares of the upper Rhine valley filled with crowds demanding
that grain be sold at what they called the old, just price.
Contemporary officials described these gatherings as blind
outbreaks of despair, and much of the subsequent historiography
has been content to repeat their verdict.
This article argues that the verdict does not survive a close
reading of the surviving record.
Far from acting on blind impulse, the crowds of 1817 followed
recognisable scripts: they seized grain, sold it at the
customary price, handed the proceeds to the merchants, and
dispersed before the militia could be assembled.

\section{Historiography}
Two interpretive traditions dominate the literature.
The older administrative histories, written from the files of
the state, treat the riots as episodes in the maintenance of
public order and measure the authorities' success by the speed
of repression.
The social histories of the postwar decades reversed the
perspective but often retained the premise, reading the crowd
as the passive instrument of hunger rather than as a political
actor with its own repertoire.
More recent work on the moral economy has restored agency to
the crowd, yet has concentrated on England and France, leaving
the smaller market towns of the German southwest largely
unexamined.
The upper Rhine valley, divided between three sovereign
territories yet integrated by a single grain market, offers
an unusually favourable setting in which to test how far
customary practices survived the territorial fragmentation
of the old regime.

\section{Sources}
The evidentiary base of the study is threefold.
First, the guild records of the bakers' and millers' corporations
preserve the day-to-day transaction prices that official
ordinances sought to regulate.
Second, the municipal account books record the extraordinary
expenditures of the riot weeks: payments to night watchmen,
compensation to merchants, and the cost of quartering troops.
Third, the correspondence of the district magistrates, preserved
in the state archive, reports the progress of each disturbance
with a frankness that official proclamations lacked.
Taken together, these sources allow the riot days to be
reconstructed hour by hour.

\section{Three Riot Days in Freiburg}
\subsection{The First Day}
The first disturbance began on a Tuesday morning, when a cart
laden with rye was stopped at the upper gate by a crowd of
perhaps two hundred persons.
The crowd did not loot the cart.
Instead, a spokesman --- identified in the magistrate's report
as a journeyman cooper named B. --- announced that the grain
would be sold at the price of the previous October.
By noon the cart stood empty, and the merchant, to his evident
surprise, received the full proceeds counted out in small coin.

\subsection{The Second Day}
The second riot, eight days later, followed the same script
with one significant variation: the crowd now included women
from the suburbs, who took charge of the improvised sale and
refused credit to known speculators.
The magistrate's informant noted that the women carried
knitting needles and kitchen knives, displayed openly but
used against no one.
The militia, mustered only in the late afternoon, found the
market square already quiet.

\subsection{The Third Day}
The third and largest gathering ended differently.
A detachment of troops arrived from the garrison town before
the customary sale could be completed, and the crowd,
after a tense hour of negotiation conducted through the
innkeeper of the Swan, agreed to disperse in exchange for
an official promise of a price ordinance.
The ordinance was published four days later and was breached
by the bakers within a fortnight, as their own ledgers show.

\section{The Kinship of the Ringleaders}
Of the fourteen persons named in the magistrate's reports,
eleven can be traced in the parish registers.
They were not marginal vagrants but settled artisans, connected
to one another by marriage and apprenticeship ties.
Two were brothers-in-law of guild masters who would later sit
in judgment over them.
This embeddedness explains both the discipline of the crowds
and the reluctance of the authorities to prosecute:
in a face-to-face society, the riot was a negotiation among
persons who expected to meet again.

\section{Ordinances and Ledgers}
A systematic comparison of the published price ordinances with
the prices actually charged, as entered in the bakers' ledgers,
shows that official regulation lagged customary enforcement
by several weeks.
Where the crowd had acted, prices fell within days and remained
low; where it had not, ordinances alone achieved little.
The ledgers thus confirm what the riot scripts suggest:
customary economy was not a memory but a working institution,
capable of disciplining the market where the state could not.

\section{Conclusion}
The grain riots of 1817 in the upper Rhine valley were neither
spasms of hunger nor rehearsals of revolution.
They were negotiated performances in which crowds, magistrates,
and merchants each played recognisable parts.
Customary economy and state paternalism, far from succeeding
one another in orderly sequence, coexisted and overlapped
well into the century of the market.
The standard narrative of a clean transition from moral to
political economy must be revised accordingly.
How far these findings travel beyond the Rhine valley is a
question for comparative work on the subsistence crises of
the 1830s and 1840s.
\end{document}
